questions.question: What is XSS? Types, impact, and how to defend against it.
questions.title: XSS — Types (Stored, Reflected, DOM) & Defenses
questions.direct_answer:
What is XSS? Types, impact, and how to defend against it.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser, network, and server contract (headers, cookies, streams)), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Stored, reflected, DOM-based XSS; output encoding, CSP, safe sinks (textContent, not innerHTML), framework auto-escaping.

**Classic weak answer:** Using dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React with user content without sanitization — a direct XSS vulnerability.

**Senior finish:** Walk through DOMPurify for sanitization; CSP nonces; trusted-types on modern browsers.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **XSS — Types (Stored, Reflected, DOM) & Defenses** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** What is XSS? Types, impact, and how to defend against it.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Stored, reflected, DOM-based XSS; output encoding, CSP, safe sinks (textContent, not innerHTML), framework auto-escaping**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Using dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React with user content without sanitization — a direct XSS vulnerability**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Walk through DOMPurify for sanitization; CSP nonces; trusted-types on modern browsers**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Stored, reflected, DOM-based XSS; output encoding, CSP, safe sinks (textContent, not innerHTML), framework auto-escaping
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

    participant I as Identity Provider

    U->>I: Authorize (PKCE / code)

    B-->>U: HttpOnly session cookie

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **using dangerouslySetInnerHTML in React with user content without sanitization — a direct XSS vulnerability** and what you do instead.

questions.question: What is CSRF? How do SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens prevent it?
questions.title: CSRF — Attacks & Defenses (SameSite, CSRF Token, Origin Header)
questions.direct_answer:
What is CSRF? How do SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens prevent it?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser, network, and server contract (headers, cookies, streams)), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** CSRF abuses browser auto-submitted cookies; defenses: SameSite=Lax/Strict (default), double-submit CSRF tokens, Origin header check.

**Classic weak answer:** Relying only on CSRF tokens without SameSite — SameSite catches most cases cheaply; tokens defend against edge cases.

**Senior finish:** Note SameSite=Lax became default in Chrome 80+ (2020); modern apps rely on it first.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on CSRF tokens without SameSite — SameSite catches most cases cheaply; tokens defend against edge cases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note SameSite=Lax became default in Chrome 80+ (2020); modern apps rely on it first

questions.question: What is Content Security Policy (CSP)? How do you configure it?
questions.title: Content Security Policy (CSP) — Nonces, strict-dynamic, Defenses
questions.direct_answer:
What is Content Security Policy (CSP)? How do you configure it?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser, network, and server contract (headers, cookies, streams)), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** HTTP header listing allowed sources; script-src, style-src, img-src, connect-src; nonce/hash or strict-dynamic for inline scripts.

**Classic weak answer:** Adding unsafe-inline to script-src — defeats XSS protection; use nonces or strict-dynamic instead.

**Senior finish:** Recommend CSP Level 3 with strict-dynamic + nonce as the modern baseline; report-uri / report-to for monitoring.
